docs.title: Pyramids QGIS
docs.text:
A QGIS plugin that exposes the pyramids GIS toolkit (pyramids-core) as a QGIS Processing provider. The algorithms appear in the Processing Toolbox under Pyramids, so they work in the toolbox, the graphical modeler, batch mode, and the Python processing.run(...) API — the same as any native QGIS algorithm.

Status: experimental

First release ships file-in / file-out raster, conversion, mesh, and Earth-observation algorithms. The raster and conversion algorithms mirror the pyramids command-line interface; the mesh and EO algorithms call their backing libraries directly (see How it works below). The plugin is marked experimental=True in its metadata.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The plugin is a thin adapter that carries no GIS logic of its own. There are two ways an algorithm reaches pyramids:

  • CLI-backed (most raster + all conversion algorithms). Each algorithm translates its QGIS parameters into a pyramids <command> ... argument list and calls the pyramids CLI in-process (pyramids.cli.main). The CLI maps 1:1 onto library calls and is pyramids' stable, documented contract, so the plugin never re-implements raster logic and never drifts from the library.
  • Library-direct (mesh + Earth-observation algorithms). Those backing packages have no CLI, so the algorithm imports and calls the library directly — UgridDataset for mesh, pyramids_eo for EO.

Work is passed by file path, never by in-memory GDAL objects: QGIS hands pyramids an input path, pyramids writes an output file, and QGIS loads it as a new layer. This deliberately avoids sharing live gdal.Dataset handles across two GDAL builds in one process.

docs.title: The dependency tiers
docs.text:
Three backing packages, three tiers of strictness, all checked in the plugin's dependencies.py:

Package Requirement Needed for pyramids-core always required (hard error if missing) every algorithm pyramids-eo required for the EO algorithms only (hard error) contrast stretch, tasseled cap pyramids-mesh optional even for the mesh algorithms (soft warning) mesh formats other than UGRID NetCDF

The critical constraint is that pyramids-core must be importable from the interpreter QGIS runs and bound to QGIS's own GDAL — not a platform wheel that vendors its own GDAL. See Installation.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Installation — install the backing libraries into QGIS's Python and deploy the plugin into a QGIS profile.
  • End-to-end testing — the by-hand validation guide: what to run, what to watch for, and when the plugin is done.
  • Algorithms — the full list of algorithms the provider ships, grouped by raster, conversion, mesh, and Earth observation.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text: Every algorithm is file-in / file-out — work is passed by file path, never by a live in-memory gdal.Dataset handle. They are grouped in the Processing Toolbox under Pyramids, by origin and theme.

docs.title: Raster
docs.text:
Most raster algorithms are CLI-backed: the plugin builds a pyramids <command> ... argument list and runs it in-process.

Algorithm pyramids command Notes Reproject raster (warp) warp target CRS + resampling Clip raster clip by polygon mask or extent Assign CRS / NoData (edit info) edit-info stamp CRS / nodata, no reprojection Merge rasters (mosaic) merge two or more inputs Raster calculator calc expression over A, B, C … (safe AST)

docs.title: Conversion
docs.text:
Also CLI-backed.

Algorithm pyramids command Notes Convert raster format convert driver from extension or explicit Rasterize (vector → raster) rasterize cell size or template grid Polygonize raster shapes one feature per cell, GeoJSON out Create Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF cog create validated COG

docs.title: Mesh
docs.text:
These wrap pyramids' UgridDataset (with pyramids-mesh providing the format drivers) rather than the CLI, since pyramids-mesh has no CLI. UGRID NetCDF is built in; other formats (2DM, Selafin, DFSU, XMDF, PLY, …) need pyramids-mesh installed.

Algorithm pyramids API Notes Convert mesh format UgridDataset.read_file / to_file any format → UGRID NetCDF or a driver Mesh to vector UgridDataset.to_geodataframe faces / nodes / edges → GeoJSON

docs.title: Earth observation
docs.text:
These wrap pyramids-eo (the EO tier on top of pyramids) directly, since it has no CLI. They need pyramids-eo installed.

Algorithm pyramids-eo API Notes Contrast stretch (EO) enhance.stretch linear / crude / cira / histogram + gamma, to dtype Tasseled cap transform spectral.tasseled_cap Landsat 5/7/8 reflectance → brightness / greenness / wetness

docs.title: Example data
docs.text: The repo ships a tiny, self-contained dataset under examples/data/ to try the algorithms on: a 32×32 EPSG:4326 DEM (dem.tif) and a polygon AOI (aoi.geojson). The same two files back the end-to-end tests in tests/integration/test_example_dataset.py. See examples/README.md for copy-paste processing.run(...) snippets.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
More of the pyramids surface is planned:

  • Auto-generate algorithms from pyramids' processing/schema.py registry (slope, aspect, hillshade, resample, sieve, fill, voronoi, quadtree, H3 …).
  • Vector-native outputs (GPKG) and multi-band / NetCDF subdataset handling.
  • STAC search / download and datacube temporal reductions.
  • An optional dock widget for interactive COG preview and STAC browsing.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: The plugin is not installed with pip install .: QGIS discovers plugins in its profile's python/plugins/ directory (by folder name + metadata.txt), not from site-packages. So you install the backing libraries into QGIS's own Python, then deploy the plugin package (src/pyramids_qgis/) into the plugins directory.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• QGIS 3.22+ (works through 4.x; the plugin uses the qgis.PyQt shim for Qt5/Qt6).
  • pyramids-core importable from QGIS's own Python, bound to QGIS's GDAL.

Do not use a vendored-GDAL wheel inside QGIS

Install pyramids into the interpreter QGIS runs — not a platform wheel that vendors its own GDAL. Those inject a private osgeo and force GDAL_DRIVER_PATH at import, which conflicts with QGIS's GDAL in-process. The plugin detects a vendored build and warns at runtime.

docs.title: 1. Clone the repo
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/serapeum-org/pyramids-qgis
cd pyramids-qgis

docs.title: 2. Install the backing libraries into QGIS's OWN Python
docs.text:
They must bind to QGIS's GDAL. pyramids-core is required; pyramids-mesh / pyramids-eo are only needed for the mesh / EO algorithms.

conda-based QGISWindows (OSGeo4W)Linux / macOS (system QGIS)

Activate the environment QGIS runs in. Install the core library from conda-forge (named pyramids, not pyramids-core); add the optional backends with pip in the same env:

conda install -c conda-forge pyramids
python -m pip install pyramids-mesh pyramids-eo   # optional: mesh / EO algorithms

Open the OSGeo4W Shell, then:

python -m pip install pyramids-core pyramids-mesh pyramids-eo

Use the interpreter QGIS runs. Find it via Plugins → Python Console: import sys; print(sys.executable), then:

<qgis-python> -m pip install pyramids-core pyramids-mesh pyramids-eo

User site vs. admin install

If you cannot write to the QGIS/OSGeo4W Python (a system or admin install), add --user so pip installs into your per-user site, which QGIS's interpreter still imports from. Avoid mixing a --user pyramids with a system one — keep a single copy on the path QGIS uses.

docs.title: What each backend unlocks
docs.text: Backend Install Enables pyramids-core required all raster / conversion algorithms; mesh on UGRID NetCDF pyramids-mesh optional the other mesh formats (2DM, Selafin, DFSU, XMDF, PLY, …) pyramids-eo optional the Earth-observation algorithms (contrast stretch, tasseled cap)

docs.title: 3. Deploy the plugin into your QGIS profile
docs.text:
From the repo root, scripts/deploy.py copies (or symlinks) src/pyramids_qgis/ into the active profile's plugins directory:

python scripts/deploy.py                        # copy into the default profile
python scripts/deploy.py --symlink              # symlink instead (dev: edits apply after a restart)
python scripts/deploy.py --profile <name>       # a non-default profile
python scripts/deploy.py --plugins-dir "<path>" # an explicit plugins dir (overrides --profile)

It installs the plugin as the folder pyramids_qgis under (default profile):

OS Plugins directory Windows %APPDATA%\QGIS\QGIS3\profiles\default\python\plugins\pyramids_qgis Linux ~/.local/share/QGIS/QGIS3/profiles/default/python/plugins/pyramids_qgis macOS ~/Library/Application Support/QGIS/QGIS3/profiles/default/python/plugins/pyramids_qgis

Manual alternative: copy or symlink src/pyramids_qgis/ into that python/plugins/ directory yourself — the installed folder must be named pyramids_qgis.

docs.title: 4. Enable and verify
docs.text:
Restart QGIS, then enable Pyramids QGIS in Plugins → Manage and Install Plugins (tick Settings → Show also experimental plugins if it is hidden — the plugin ships experimental=True). The algorithms then appear in the Processing Toolbox under Pyramids.

If nothing shows up, open Plugins → Python Console and read the error — it is almost always a missing pyramids-core in QGIS's own Python (step 2).

Once the plugin loads, work through the end-to-end testing guide to confirm the algorithms actually run on real data.

docs.title: End-to-end testing
docs.text:
The unit / integration suite runs against real PyQGIS in CI and exercises every algorithm's initAlgorithm / parameter construction. What it does not cover is running an algorithm end-to-end (processAlgorithm) in a real QGIS session on real data, nor the GUI / dialog behaviour. That still has to be done by hand, and it is the gate before a non-experimental release.

This page is that by-hand validation guide. Install the plugin first — see Installation.

docs.title: What to run — cover both wiring paths and all four groups
docs.text:
The raster / conversion algorithms call the pyramids CLI in-process; the mesh / EO ones call the library directly. Run at least one of each path:

  • [ ] Raster (CLI path): Reproject (warp) a GeoTIFF to another CRS; confirm the output layer loads and looks right.
  • [ ] Raster: Clip (by mask and by extent), Merge, Raster calculator (e.g. NDVI over two inputs), Assign CRS / NoData.
  • [ ] Conversion: Rasterize a vector, Polygonize a raster (GeoJSON output), Create COG, Convert format.
  • [ ] Mesh (library path): Convert a .2dm / Selafin mesh to UGRID NetCDF, and Mesh → vector (needs pyramids-mesh).
  • [ ] EO (library path): Contrast stretch, and Tasseled cap on a Landsat reflectance stack (needs pyramids-eo).

docs.title: What to watch for — things CI cannot catch
docs.text:
• [ ] PyQGIS parameter wiring — each algorithm's parameterAs* calls, enum / attribute names, and the dialog rendering. (initAlgorithm / parameter construction is covered automatically by the real-QGIS integration tests; the dialog rendering and actual execution are not.)
  • [ ] Forced-GeoJSON output — the provider pins vector outputs to .geojson; confirm Polygonize / Mesh → vector produce loadable GeoJSON and the extension matches the content.
  • [ ] Dependency guards — with pyramids-mesh / pyramids-eo absent, the mesh / EO algorithms should raise a clear "install ..." message; the vendored-GDAL warning should appear only for a vendored build.
  • [ ] Error surfacing — a bad CRS / missing file should come back as a clean QgsProcessingException in the Processing log, not a raw traceback.
  • [ ] Qt5 / Qt6 — ideally smoke-test on a QGIS 3.x (Qt5) and a 4.x (Qt6) build, since the plugin uses the qgis.PyQt shim.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• [ ] At least one algorithm per group runs successfully on real data and loads a correct output layer.
  • [ ] The dependency-guard and error-surfacing behaviour is confirmed.
  • [ ] Any bugs found are filed as their own issues (and fixed) before flipping experimental=False in metadata.txt.

docs.title: Change-log
docs.text:
The project's change-log is generated by commitizen from the Conventional Commit history on each release (cz bump, run by the github-release workflow) and written to CHANGELOG.md at the repo root. It is not edited by hand — any manual change is overwritten on the next release.

The first tagged release populates it from the commit history to date. Until then, see the commit history and the Releases page on GitHub.
